summary.text: 京 is interpreted as a picture of a tall building or platform; the Shuowen account instead describes a high man-made mound. Its common present meaning is “capital,” but the evidence does not establish how that sense arose from the earlier interpretations.

formation.text: Treat 京 as a whole pictograph of a tall built structure or platform. The Shuowen account offers a competing high-mound explanation; neither interpretation establishes a dated route to “capital.”

components.text: 京 is treated as one pictorial graph, not split into modern-looking parts. Paleographic descriptions interpret early forms as a roof, tower, and wall; the selected oracle-style glyph is a modern redraw, not an ancient artifact.

history.text: The selected oracle-bone-style redraw has a broad rooflike top, a central opening, and three downward strokes. It illustrates the building interpretation but is not a dated inscription and cannot establish the graph’s original meaning.

Paleographic accounts interpret the oracle-bone and bronze forms as a tall building. They describe the small-seal form as simplifying the tower element to 口; this is their interpretation, not a dated demonstration of that graphic change.

uncertainties.text: 京 has competing interpretations as a tall building or platform and as a high man-made mound. A hilltop shrine or settlement has also been proposed to explain “capital,” but the route to that sense remains unresolved.
The evidence does not date the earliest use of 京 for “capital” or show whether it developed from a mound or settlement sense, followed another path, or represents a distinct word sense.

senses.text: 京 is interpreted as a tall building or platform; the Shuowen account instead describes a high man-made mound. The evidence does not resolve which interpretation best captures its earliest meaning.

senses.period: attested in a Tang poem by cited work; earliest use unresolved
senses.text: 京 means “capital city”; an example occurs in a cited Tang poem. This does not establish when the sense began or how it relates to the high-structure or mound interpretations.
“Large” is recorded as a sense, but its chronology and connection to the other meanings are not established.

limitations.text: The evidence does not establish a chronological semantic link between the high-structure or mound interpretations and “capital” or “large.”

overview.text: 京 is interpreted as a picture of a tall building or high platform. It commonly means “capital” today, though the path from the earlier interpretations to that sense is unresolved.

components.text: Read 京 as one picture of a tall built form; its visible parts are not treated as separate components here.
